newsitem.title: FRANCE: FORECAST-French data to show uneven growth pattern.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-French data to show uneven growth pattern.

text.p: A batch of French economic figures due to be released next week is expected to underline the uneven pattern of growth so far in 1996 while pointing to a slight improvement early next year, economists said on Friday.

The first estimate of third-quarter growth was expected to show a rebound from the second quarter, but October consumer spending figures were seen down, as spending on cars trailed off with the expiry of a government incentive scheme in September.

Still, most economists said a November survey of French industrialists would probably show fewer businesses were expecting future output to decline, following on from a less pessimistic October survey.

"We have a very uneven pattern of growth," Joanne Perez, strategist at Merrill Lynch in Paris, said. The improvement in consumption in the third quarter was unlikely to be sustained but, at the same time, there were signs businesses are becoming less worried, she said.

Third-quarter gross domestic product was expected to climb 0.9 percent from the second quarter, according to the median forecast of 10 economists polled by Reuters. The range of forecasts was 0.7 percent to 1.3 percent.
The majority of those economists who gave a forecast for consumer spending on manufactured goods in October, however, predicted a decline, with two expecting a 2.0 percent drop.

The consumption report was scheduled for release on Tuesday at 0750 GMT by national statistics institute INSEE. The industry survey was due on Wednesday and the GDP estimate on Thursday, both at 0745 GMT.
Economists said the engine of growth in the third quarter was consumer spending on manufactured goods, seen in a strong 3.4 percent rise in August driven chiefly by car sales.
All the economists who gave a forecast for overall consumption in the third quarter estimated a rise in the range of 1.2 percent to 1.5 percent.
"We should come back from the weakness in the second quarter with much stronger consumption for auto sales," said Sonja Gibbs, analyst at Nomura International.
"Overall, the numbers should be showing signs of recovery, but I don't think people will be see inflation risks with the growth, so they should be quite good for markets," Gibbs said.

Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston, said the GDP figure was difficult to predict accurately because of the distortion to consumption from car sales and because of the fact there were more working days in the quarter, which may have boosted the overall figure.
Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro in Paris, said he expected a 0.5 percent rise in investment in the third quarter growth to help the headline figure.
He said he expected no negative or positive contribution from changes in stock levels, and that trade might have a small negative impact on growth.

Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley, predicted a strong 1.3 percent rise in investment and a positive contribution from trade, in addition to a consumption, to produce a 1.3 percent rise in GDP, the highest forecast in the poll.
